chunks.text: IV Discussion Table 2: Four discovery types used in this work. Reflection on Types I-III motivated this work. Type IV was added retrospectively during the human–AI analysis. The classification is contextual rather than absolute: the same result can change type as the state of scientific awareness changes. Type Operational meaning I Solve a long-standing known unknown (KU). II Reveal a remote unknown unknown (UU). III Systematically develop a landscape opened by I, II, or IV, leading to new I/II/IV breakthroughs. IV Recognize an unknown known (UK). IV.1 Organizing human-AI research We first describe the conceptual framework that motivated this work and was subsequently refined by its outcomes. The recognition problem led to a context-dependent classification that now comprises four broad types: Types I–III motivated the present study, while Type IV emerged in hindsight and then gave rise to the fourth axis of the AHS, as the black axis illustrated in Fig. 1 . Type I solves a longstanding problem—a known unknown (KU). Type II reveals an unknown unknown (UU) that is far beyond the existing AHS. Type III systematically develops the landscape opened by Type-I, Type-II, or Type-IV discoveries through exploration, development, generalization, connection, and application, thereby creating conditions for subsequent Type-I, Type-II, or Type-IV breakthroughs. Type IV recognizes an unknown known (UK): a latent connection among already available ingredients. A repeated pattern of III → \to I/II/IV → \to new III → \to new I/II/IV → ⋯ \to\cdots forms a helix of discovery. Table 2 summarizes this terminology. The classification focuses on well-documented timestamped recognition problems rather than less objective measures of difficulty or significance. Because a Type-I KU is longstanding, it can contain something beyond the AHS; its resolution can reveal Type-II breakthroughs.

Conversely, recognizing a Type-II UU can drive a Type-I breakthrough and sometimes even make a Type-I puzzle appear easy in the expanded AHS. In comparison, Type-III-stage KUs can be easier to identify and quicker to solve, resulting in two important ingredients: data and the implications of the data. Deep insight into those results provides an operational pathway to new AHS and next Type-I/II/IV breakthroughs. Figure 2: Schematics of (a) a 9d one-shot autonomous Type-I route vs (b) the human-AI co-development approach, where the research state, active context, and the agents’ roles are progressively updated as the research evolves from an initial Type-III AHS towards Type-I/II/IV breakthroughs. Both approaches start with intelligence equipped with known knowns (KKs). We then translated the second, methodological question as follows: can human–AI research be organized systematically so that AI participation in Type-III development increases the chance of reaching next Type-I/II/IV breakthroughs—by producing results whose deeper implications can subsequently be recognized by the human or the AI? To address this question about the AI’s role, we proposed a nine-dan AI-contribution framework [ 8 ] to replace a vague statement such as “AI assisted this research.” The framework is divided into two groups: (1) 1d through 5d, in which the human can complete the study without the AI and the AI is employed to dramatically accelerate the project, and (2) 6d through 9d, in which the human cannot complete the study without the AI and the AI acts as a scientific discoverer and an inspirational research partner. In the organization used here, levels one dan to five dan (1d–5d) form a Type-III track and levels 6d–9d a Type-I/II track, each with increasing autonomy and scientific impact. The newly added Type IV is primarily a recognition-oriented discovery and, when contributed by AI, can be assigned 2d or 6d depending on the AI’s role.

In this work, the Potts Type-IV recognition is therefore classified as 6d, whereas the Type-IV extension to arbitrary inhomogeneous interactions arose from the human’s recognition of the implications of the AI-generated microscopic proof. If Type III is the cradle of Types I/II/IV, sustained AI participation in Type III—with progressive 1d–5d contributions—may likewise be a cradle for 6d–9d scientific performance, including autonomous hypothesis generation outside the AHS. Now for practical purposes we find it is necessary to distinguish an active problem space (APS) from an AHS. Problem statements define an APS, not necessarily an AHS. An AHS begins when concrete candidate explanations, representations, mechanisms, or solution routes are being actively entertained. This clarifies why Type III matters in this human-AI co-development approach. Type III does not merely keep the AI busy. It creates an actual AHS by progressively developing concrete structure. Operationally, we do not reveal the whole human APS to the AI, and only select those problems that the human can use to design the initial AHS. If the AI solves or makes a significant step in solving unreleased problems in the human APS—for which the human could not form an AHS—during the AHS course, that is an operationally identifiable event of AI going outside the AHS. Further, if the problems are outside the human APS, that could be a strong indicator of AI-driven or AI-led breakthroughs. Hence, the longitudinal human–AI co-development should be distinguished from one-shot autonomous problem solving: here the research state, active context, the agents’ roles are progressively updated, as illustrated in Fig. 2 . At the center of this Y-shaped workflow is a human-designed initial Type-III AHS for AI to develop and maintain task-relevant scientific context across a progression of real research problems.

In the 1d–5d Type-III track used here, the selected KUs are problems that the human could in principle complete without the AI; therefore, the AI can be well mentored. In this setting, the AI is expected not only to accelerate the project but also to generate hypotheses outside the AHS because of its broad knowledge base and its ability to connect representations and synthesize solution methods. The human remains engaged throughout to recognize the implications of the AI results and update the AHS accordingly. Like in a Socratic dialogue, the solution, or even the problem, emerges from the human-AI conversation. This makes a difference in practice: For a Type-I APS-centered approach, one may prefer the highest-performance reasoning option. By contrast, in a Type-III AHS-centered approach, a nonmaximal reasoning mode with faster response, better suited to sustaining rapid human–AI iteration, may be preferable. For example, among the five reasoning options available in our ChatGPT 5.6 interface at the time of this study— Instant , Medium , High , Extra High , and Pro —we used High for discovery and Extra High for critical manuscript review. IV.2 Human-AI research trajectory The physics progression and the AI-contribution progression are related but not identical. The discovery type describes what occurred relative to the scientific landscape; the dan level in Ref. [ 8 ] describes what role AI played in that particular research step. Fig. 1 illustrates the physics progression as an expansion from a single point [ 1 ] to a four-axis AHS: model choice from Potts to O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) , system size L L , homogeneous arbitrary interactions, and inhomogeneity. Fig. 3 records the human–AI co-development trajectory and the main AI-contribution episodes. The two figures share the same AHS color scheme; thus, the physics progression and the AI-contribution progression can be compared.

IV.2.2 AI-reshaped AHS and a Type-I/II breakthrough During the Type-III development, the AI independently encountered the Hamiltonian-level mapping problem through the literature, brought it into its own APS, and produced a Hamiltonian-level proof for n = 3 n=3 , thereby overcoming the 1990 stated challenge [ 28 ] , a Type-I discovery. Thus, it was the AI who led the Hamiltonian-level mapping problem to the shared human–AI APS. This pivoted the research by introducing a new 1 / L 1/L axis to the AHS (red axis in Fig. 1 ; red rounded rectangle in Fig. 3 ), a Type-II. The AI contribution was temporally assigned 6d AI-reshaped and would be readjusted by its subsequent performance. The human recognized its potential and then conjectured an O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) microscopic mapping (red plane in Fig. 1 ; red rounded rectangle on the human side in Fig. 3 ). The actual prompt was “Hi buddy, for the clock, XY, and Heisenberg models there is a remarkably clean microscopic geometric derivation, which exposes the mapping at the Hamiltonian level and a strong finite-size mapping for the partition functions for the open chains. This seems to hold for n n -vector spins for all n n and arbitrary interaction functions.” Note that the AI-generated arbitrary- U , V U,V result had by then already entered the shared AHS and had been adopted by this prompt. Then, the AI synthesized the recursive Householder moving-frame method to derive the proof, a Type-II discovery, classified as 9d under the definitions of Ref. [ 8 ] . One may argue that, since the human made a prompt, the AI contribution was not 9d AI-led but closer to 8d AI-driven. This provides a useful case study of the context-dependent nature of the nine-dan framework. 8d is the case in which AI autonomously generalizes human-supplied seed examples to the full solution. Here, the critical seed example—the Hamiltonian-level proof for n = 3 n=3 —was supplied by the AI, not by the human.

Hence, the AI solved a conjecture with its own seed and full solution; its contribution was clearly beyond 8d. Moreover, the Hamiltonian-level proof problem was introduced to the shared human-AI APS by the AI, while it had been hidden in the human’s private APS. Therefore the 9d AI-led assessment was not an exaggeration but a rational action. IV.2.3 Inhomogeneity, a Type-IV breakthrough Finally, the human recognized the implication of the geometry-based microscopic proof—which acts on the arguments of the interaction functions, not the interactions themselves—and introduced arbitrary inhomogeneous interaction functions. This expands the AHS to the fourth axis from the homogeneous specialization (black axis in Fig. 1 ; black rounded rectangle in Fig. 3 ) with no need to modify the proof—a Type-IV recognition breakthrough. This immediately brings a broader class of inhomogeneous geometries within the theorem, after a suitable one-dimensional ordering, including regular two-leg ladders, bond- and site-decorated chains, dimerized chains, and disordered chains, obtained by appropriate site dependence or vanishing of selected U i U_{i} and V i V_{i} . IV.3 Potts implication and Type-IV discovery Moreover, the intermediate 6d AI-reshaped event generated another autonomous microscopic proof for the q q -state standard Potts chain (the first red rounded rectangle). This not only closes a knowledge gap but also provides an ideal illustration of the recognition problem: precisely because the solution is so simple, it exposes a broader lesson about representation. Historically, the q q -state Potts model was introduced as a simpler generalization of the Ising model than the planar q q -state model now known as the clock model [ 22 ] . It is invariant under any permutation of the q q Potts states. Exploiting the 𝕊 q \mathbb{S}_{q} symmetry or the 𝕊 q − 1 \mathbb{S}_{q-1} symmetry in a field that selects one state, say P P , has taken the center stage.

For example, the 2025 thermodynamic mapping was obtained by using 𝕊 q \mathbb{S}_{q} symmetry to reduce the q 2 × q 2 q^{2}\times q^{2} transfer matrix of the J 1 J_{1} - J 2 J_{2} Potts chain to the 2 × 2 2\times 2 maximally symmetric subspace (MSS) containing the largest eigenvalue and matching it to the 2 × 2 2\times 2 MSS of the q q -state J J - h h Potts chain due to 𝕊 q − 1 \mathbb{S}_{q-1} symmetry [ 1 ] . The labeling of the Potts states including P P has no physical meaning—they can be named arbitrarily. For example, the Potts states were conventionally labeled by σ i ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , q − 1 } \sigma_{i}\in\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\} and P = 0 P=0 [ 25 , 38 ] or σ i ∈ { 1 , 2 ​ … , q } \sigma_{i}\in\{1,2\ldots,q\} and P = 1 P=1 [ 1 , 30 ] with no rule imposed for their relative relationship. However, this is now recognized to be the blind spot in finding a microscopic mapping. In the present workflow, the recognition breakthrough itself followed the human-designed Type-III research. We deliberately stopped at an intermediate q q -dimensional invariant subspace instead of the 2 × 2 2\times 2 MSS (see Supplemental Material II.A). This weaker reduction is already sufficient to prove the thermodynamic mapping and is also the step that survives for the clock model and continuous vector spins—it was the actual starting point of the initial AHS (Fig. 3 the topmost green arrow marked by q 2 → q q^{2}\to q ). The reduced q × q q\times q transfer matrix and the mapping are certainly independent of how the Potts states are labeled, as verified by the human using symbolic derivation within the Wolfram Mathematica 14.3 software package for q = 2 − 10 q=2-10 before releasing the initial AHS to the AI. However, unlike the easily comparable MSS (having only four elements), the q × q q\times q space demands an efficient, analytic way for bookkeeping and comparing the matrix elements for arbitrary q q .

This drove the AI to exploit those labels as elements of ℤ q \mathbb{Z}_{q} , with subtraction modulo q q , as the relative variables needed for the mapping. Later on, the AI autonomously recognized its use in the microscopic mapping; the auxiliary ℤ q \mathbb{Z}_{q} labeling of the Potts states does not alter the physical 𝕊 q \mathbb{S}_{q} invariance of the original zero-field Hamiltonian, while the mapped field model has the expected 𝕊 q − 1 \mathbb{S}_{q-1} symmetry fixing P P . This cyclic labeling with a strict subtraction rule is not just another convenient coordinate choice, but the mathematical bridge to connect the two models microscopically at the Hamiltonian level. In a broader sense, the discovery tells us something about the organization of knowledge: apparently neighboring facts can remain disconnected because they are expressed in incompatible representations. The Potts model demonstrates a central lesson that unifies all the pieces of discovery in this work: the correct local variable can be hidden in the conventional representation. For Potts, the conventional permutation-symmetric 𝕊 q \mathbb{S}_{q} description does not expose the relevant subtraction structure. For O ⁡ ( 3 ) O(3) , laboratory-frame spin coordinates hide the bond-relative geometry. For general O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) , a fixed global coordinate system hides the recursive local frame. In every case, once the appropriate relative-coordinate representation is recognized, the Hamiltonian reorganizes itself.

That lesson gives the Householder result extra significance: it is not merely an O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) generalization of an Ising or Potts trick, but a systematic answer to the question that the Potts episode dramatizes: How do we construct the relative variables that reveal hidden Hamiltonian equivalences? With these insights, the Potts lesson suggests a redefinition of “unknown knowns” (UK) as the fourth type of discovery to recognize that a scientific result may remain inaccessible not because the ingredients are unknown or the computation is difficult, but because the relevant known ingredients are encoded in representations that conceal their connection. Type-IV knowledge connection is distinct from Type-II knowledge synthesis: Type IV recognizes a latent connection among already available ingredients, whereas Type II introduces a genuinely new relation lying far beyond the relevant AHS. As demonstrated above, Type-IV recognition can seed new Type-I, Type-II, and Type-III developments while also providing a unifying interpretation of earlier results. Type IV ties directly to AI: a sufficiently broad reasoning system may be unusually well-suited for representation switching and cross-domain connection. Here, the ℤ q \mathbb{Z}_{q} cyclic labeling is well known in the context of the clock model, which possesses the ℤ q \mathbb{Z}_{q} symmetry rather than 𝕊 q \mathbb{S}_{q} [ 22 , 27 ] . It has even been used to map the 1D standard Potts model with multi-site interactions onto a standard 2D Potts model [ 39 ] . Yet, to recognize this as a Type IV for the Hamiltonian-level J 1 J_{1} - J 2 J_{2} ↔ \leftrightarrow J J - h h mapping, the problem must first be cast into the APS and AHS. The AI did so exactly and autonomously. Explicitly recognizing Type IV as a discovery mode may accelerate the identification of UKs.

The last step of this work could be an example: the human’s timely recognition of arbitrary inhomogeneous interactions added a new fourth axis to the AHS—black axis in Fig. 1 —with no need to modify the proof. IV.4 External comparison The May 2026 autonomous resolution of the Erdős planar unit-distance problem provides a useful external comparison [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . There the open problem was already known and selected, making the event a particularly clear Type-I autonomous breakthrough. The general-purpose reasoning model was not specially trained for that mathematical problem but evaluated across a collection of Erdős problems—effectively an APS, rather than being supplied with a problem-specific AHS—and it unexpectedly found a successful route using sophisticated algebraic-number-theoretic ideas [ 2 ] . The present case probes both a complementary route and a similar route: the initial AHS did not contain an arbitrary-interaction conjecture and a microscopic proof conjecture, but the AI worked on a collection of Type-III thermodynamic mapping problems. It enlarged the AHS while participating in the development of a much narrower theorem. In that sense, the homogeneous U , V U,V result is Type II, while the n = 3 n=3 microscopic proof qualifies as both Type I and Type II: Type I because it overcame the 1990 stated obstruction, and Type II because its constructive route lay far beyond the human AHS. The subsequent O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) Householder construction generalized this result after the human formulated the O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) hypothesis. The geometric proof may be viewed as a synthesis of two familiar ideas: the ordered propagation characteristic of one-dimensional transfer constructions and the Householder reflection of numerical linear algebra.

The cumulative frame 𝖦 i = 𝖦 1 𝖧 ( 𝝈 1 ) H ( 𝝈 2 ) ⋯ 𝖧 ( 𝝈 i − 1 ) \mathsf{G}_{i}=\mathsf{G}_{1}\mathsf{H}(\bm{\sigma}_{1})H(\bm{\sigma}_{2})\cdots\mathsf{H}(\bm{\sigma}_{i-1}) transports local bond geometry along the chain, converting the NNN scalar product of the original spins into the NN scalar product of the transformed spins. This cross-domain synthesis is reminiscent, at a methodological level, of those recent AI-generated mathematical discoveries in which established tools from a distant field were brought unexpectedly to bear on a longstanding problem [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . These events illustrate why autonomous hypothesis generation deserves separate attention from autonomous problem solving and how they are connected in one project. Maximizing single-shot reasoning power and maximizing longitudinal co-development efficiency are not necessarily the same optimization problem. Together, they sharpen the practical question: rather than waiting for isolated spectacular successes, can a research process be designed to cultivate the conditions from which such high-autonomy contributions emerge? Last but not least, the developmental hypothesis provided by this paper is only a proof of concept, not a causal demonstration that continuous Type-III involvement will generally produce Type-I/II/IV contributions. A single longitudinal case cannot establish an incidence rate, a necessary sequence of dan levels, or a universal relationship between discovery type and contribution level. The four discovery types are contextual, and the dan labels are task-level attributions. A rigorous research program in understanding the effectiveness of this approach should therefore test the hypothesis prospectively across multiple domains, with complete human–AI interaction records, predefined criteria for provenance and novelty, adversarial validation, and comparison against workflows in which AI participation is intentionally interrupted.
We anticipate more reports of human–AI research conducted in the proposed Type-III-based discovery framework.
